To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
scrolling Web pages can reduce comprehension of complex texts.

1) scrolling Web pages reduced learning from complex topics for readers who were low in working memory capacity; and 2) the scrolling format did not affect the learning of high working memory capacity readers or the learning of all readers when reading simpler topics.
scrolling Web pages reduce comprehension of complex texts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the presentation of information on a Web page affects comprehension, especially for readers with low working memory capacity.
the effects of scrolling Web pages on comprehension of complex text for readers who differ with respect to working memory capacity.
how users of complex information systems, such as the Web, can best be supported in their interactions with these systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
scrolling is a poor way to present text, particularly if the text is complex and/or the reader has a limited working memory capacity.
the way in which information is presented can affect learning.

the way in which text is presented on a screen can have an effect on comprehension, and that the way in the which text is presented can affect the learning outcomes of readers who vary in their working memory capacities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of scrolling interfaces on comprehension are moderated by working memory capacity.
scrolling interfaces may not always be the best way to present information.
the way in which information is presented can affect learning outcomes and that the way in is presented can interact in important ways with the characteristics of the learner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
scrolling interfaces can have negative effects on comprehension for some readers.
the scrolling format should be avoided when conveying complex content to readers who are lower in working memory.
the way that information is presented can affect the way people learn.
